title: Book 6 — Erato, Chapter 12
paragraphs: Hearing this, the Ionians handed themselves over to Dionysius; and he used to bring the ships out every day in single file, so that he might train the rowers by making the ships break through one another's line, and so that he might get the fighting-men on the ships under arms; and then for the rest of the day he would keep the ships at anchor. In this way he gave the Ionians work to do all day long. For seven days they submitted and did what he commanded; but on the next day the Ionians, being unaccustomed to such toils and exhausted by hard work and hot sun, said to one another: “Against which of the gods have we offended, that we so fill up the measure of our misery? For surely we have handed ourselves over to a Phocaean, a charlatan, who furnishes only three ships; and he has taken us into his hands and maltreats us with evil dealing from which we can never recover. Many of us, in fact, have fallen into sickness, and many others may be expected to suffer the same thing shortly; and for us it is better to endure anything else in the world rather than these ills, and to undergo the slavery that will come upon us, whatever it may be, rather than to be oppressed by what we have now. Come, let us obey him no more.” So they said; and forthwith, after this, each refused to obey him, and they pitched their tents on the island like an army, and kept in the shade, and would not go on board their ships or carry out any drills.
